docs.title: The Contour Integral Method (CIM) Tool
docs.text: CIMTOOL is a graphical user interface created for the exploration and application of contour integral methods to solve eigenvalue problems.

docs.title: NSF Award Information
docs.text: This project is supported by the National Science Foundation Grant DMS-241141, Nonlinear eigenvalue problems: A new paradigm through the lens of systems theory and rational interpolation, Co-PIs: M. Embree and S. Gugercin, Aug 1, 2024 – July 31, 2027

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import Visual.*;
%
n = OperatorData([],'omnicam1');
c = Contour.Circle(0.4,0.2,8);
cim = CIM(n,c);
%
cim.SampleData.ell = 3; cim.SampleData.r = 3;
cim.RealizationData.RealizationSize = Numerics.RealizationSize(3,3);
cim.RealizationData.ComputationalMode = Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner;
%
CTOOL = CIMTOOL(cim)

Check out additional scripts and demos under src/tutorial or src/demos.

docs.title: GUI.SubObjectListener
docs.text:
A PostSet listener on a property of an object reached from a root through a property path, such as Prop of cim.SampleData.Contour for the path "SampleData.Contour". When any object along the path is replaced, the listener moves to the new object and the callback runs once, so a GUI component that reads the current object stays in sync. An empty path listens on the root itself. A target without the property gets no listener until a replacement brings one that has it; the callback then still runs once and must handle that case.

Usage

l = GUI.SubObjectListener(cim, "SampleData.Contour", 'N', @(~,~) comp.QuadratureChangedFcn([])); delete(l); % removes every listener it holds

docs.title: Miscellaneous
docs.text:
Numerical rank of Db: the number of singular values at or above the larger of abstol and reltolsigma_1, or above max(size(Db))eps(sigma_1) when both are NaN.

Size of the contour moments sum_j w_j s_j^k Q(:,:,j), k = 0..kmax, relative to their bound max|Q|*sum|w|, where s_j = (z_j - c)/max|z - c| maps the nodes z into the unit disk around their mean c. The moments vanish, up to quadrature and roundoff error, when the contour encloses no eigenvalue, so a level near eps marks an empty contour. Moments beyond k = 0 keep a polynomial problem with all its eigenvalues enclosed, whose k = 0 moment cancels, from reading as empty. Q holds one sample per node along its third dimension.

Numerical rank of a matrix from its singular values Sigma (as returned by svd): the m with the largest ratio sigma_m/sigma_{m+1}, after raising each singular value to the floor max(size(Sigma))*eps(sigma_1) of Numerics.rankdet, so exact zeros and the roundoff tail tie. ratio is that largest ratio (Inf for a single singular value, NaN when sigma_1 = 0); m = 0 when Sigma is empty or zero.

  • L –

    \( n \times \ell \) matrix of left probing directions

  • R –

    \( n \times r \) matrix of right probing directions

  • theta –

    left interpolation points

  • sigma –

    right interpolation points

  • m –

    number of poles to search for in \( \Omega \)

Name-value arguments:

  • PadStrategy –

    padding strategy for construction of BB/CC (if the number of left/right tangential directions is less than the number of corresponding interpolation points)

  • Verbose –

    verbose output (or not)

docs.title: Enumerations
docs.text:
• Hankel: Essentially Probed Eigenvalue Realization Algorithm (ERA).

  • Direct: Sampling the operator via numerical integration directly.

The rule applies when RealizationData.AutoRank is true; otherwise m is RealizationSize.m.

Builds the data matrices (as computeDataMatrices), then realizes them at RealizationSize.m or, under RealizationData.AutoRank, at the m that RealizationData.RankRule chooses: the numerical rank of Db under the tolerances in options (Tolerance), or its largest singular-value gap (Gap). docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Quadratic eigenvalue problem (QEP) that arises from the wave equation on \( [0, 1] \):

\[ \frac{d^2 p}{d x^2} + 4 \pi^2 \lambda^2 p = 0, \quad p(0) = 0, \quad \chi p'(1) + 2 \pi i \lambda p(1) = 0. \]

\(p\) is the acoustic pressure, \( \lambda \) is the frequency, and \( \chi \) is the impedance.

We aim to find eigenpairs \( (\lambda,\vec{x}) \) such that

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda) \vec{x} = \vec{0} \]

where

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda) = \lambda^2 \mathbf{M} + \lambda \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{K}, \quad \mathbf{M},\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}. \]

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
We put \( N = 506 \), \( \chi = 1.0001 \), and let \( \Omega = \mathcal{B}(0.8i,10) \) be the circular contour centered at \( \gamma = 0.8i \) with radius \( \rho = 10 \) and 512 quadrature nodes.

Code (operator and contour) 
N = 506; Xi = 1.0001;
n = Visual.OperatorData([], 'acoustic_wave_1d', sprintf("%f,%f", N, Xi));
c = Visual.Contour.Circle(0.8i, 10, 512);
cim = Visual.CIM(n, c);

Reference eigenvalues can be computed explicitly as

\[ \lambda_k = \frac{\tan^{-1}(i \chi)}{2 \pi} + \frac{k}{2}, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z} \]

when \( \tan^{-1}(i \chi) \) is defined.

Code (reference eigenvalues) 
% the eigenvalues of the continuous problem
n.refew = atan(1i*Xi)/(2*pi) + (-50:50).'/2;

\( \mathbf{T} \) is meromorphic with \( m = 40 \) simple poles in \( \Omega \). Hankel and MPLoewner-based CIMs build up relevant data matrices and utilize a rank-\( m \) truncated SVD, where, with exact data, \( m \) is exactly the number of poles of \( \mathbf{T} \) within \( \Omega \) (counting multiplicities). Inexact data is derived through contour integration of \( f_k(z) \left( \left[ \mathbf{T}(z) \right]^{-1} \right) \), approximated via quadrature rule. \( f_k(z) \) depends on the choice of Hankel/SPLoewner/MPLoewner formulations and, in the case of the latter two, on the choice of shift \( \sigma \). In practice, left (\( \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times \ell} \)) and right (\( \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times r} \)) probing matrices are used to reduce the computational burden of full inversion of \( \mathbf{T} \) at each quadrature node, so that the integrand becomes \( f_k(z) \left( \mathbf{L}^* \left[ \mathbf{T}(z) \right]^{-1} \mathbf{R} \right) \).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
We set \( \ell = r = 15 \) and choose \( K \) so that \( \mathbb{D},\mathbb{D_s} \in \mathbb{C}^{60 \times 60} \). With AutoRank, the realization order \( m \) sits at the largest gap in the singular values of \( \mathbb{D} \).

Code (probing directions and realization order) 
p = 15; cim.SampleData.ell = p; cim.SampleData.r = p;
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;   % m at the largest gap in the singular values of Db

docs.title: Hankel
docs.text:
To use Hankel realization, we specify it and the number of moments \( K \) used to build \( \mathbb{D} \).

Code (Hankel realization) 
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.Hankel, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 4));   % Db is 60 x 60
cim.compute();
fprintf('Hankel: m = %d, max relative residual %.1e\n', cim.ResultData.m, cim.maxrelresidual());

The gap falls at \( m = 42 \): the 40 eigenvalues inside \( \Omega \) and two just outside it, at \( \pm 10.003 + 0.555i \). The maximum relative residual (MRR) of the 42 computed eigenpairs is \( 1.9\times10^{-13} \).

docs.title: MPLoewner
docs.text:
We switch computational modes to MPLoewner where \( K \) now represents the number of shifts used in construction of \( \mathbb{D} \).

Code (MPLoewner realization) 
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 4*p));   % Db is 60 x 60
cim.compute();
fprintf('MPLoewner: m = %d, max relative residual %.1e\n', cim.ResultData.m, cim.maxrelresidual());

MPLoewner also realizes \( m = 42 \) eigenvalues, with MRR \( 1.2\times10^{-14} \). The demo src/demos/acoustic_wave_1d.m also opens the CIMTOOL GUI on cim.

  1. F. Chaitin-Chatelin and M. B. van Gijzen, “Analysis of parameterized quadratic eigenvalue problems in computational acoustics with homotopic deviation theory,” Numerical Linear Algebra with Applications, vol. 13, no. 6, pp. 487–512, 2006, doi: 10.1002/nla.484. ↩

docs.title: Time-Delay Eigenvalue Problems
docs.text:
Many physical systems carry a time delay \( \tau \): a signal, a wave, or a measurement arrives some time after it is produced. When systems incorporate a delay, it is often of interest to determine for which delay the system becomes unstable i.e. to determine the stability margin of the system. For continuous-time systems, this is given by the smallest \( \tau \) such that poles of the system have zero real part. A general delay system can be written in the following form

\[ \mathbf{E}\dot{x}(t) = \varphi\big(t, x(t), x(\kappa(t)), \dot{x}(\kappa(t))\big), \qquad \kappa_i(t) = t - \tau_i, \quad i = 1, 2, \dots, k_m . \]

where \( \tau = \left[ \tau_1, \ldots, \tau_{k_m} \right]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{k_m} \) is a set of constant delays. When \( \phi \) depends only on the first three arguments, we say that that the system is retarded and, otherwise, we say that it is neutral. Below are two examples of such systems with only a single delay

\[ \underbrace{\mathbf{E}\dot{x}(t) = \mathbf{A}_0 x(t) + \mathbf{A}_1 x(t-\tau)}_{\text{retarded}} \qquad \underbrace{\mathbf{E}_0\dot{x}(t) + \mathbf{E}_1\dot{x}(t-\tau) = \mathbf{A}_0 x(t) + \mathbf{A}_1 x(t-\tau)}_{\text{neutral}} . \]

Seeking solutions of the form \( x(t) = e^{\lambda t}\vec{v} \) turns the stability question for these systems into a nonlinear eigenvalue problem \( \mathbf{T}(\lambda, \tau)\,\vec{v} = 0 \). After some algebraic manipulations, the above equations become

\[ \underbrace{\mathbf{T}(\lambda,\tau) = \lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}_0 - \mathbf{A}_1 e^{-\lambda\tau}}_{\text{retarded}} \qquad \underbrace{\mathbf{T}(\lambda,\tau) = \lambda(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{E}_1 e^{-\lambda\tau}) - \mathbf{A}_0 - \mathbf{A}_1 e^{-\lambda\tau}}_{\text{neutral}} . \]

Unlike polynomial or rational eigenvalue problems, these are transcendental in \( \lambda \); there are infinitely many eigenvalues, and no exact, finite linearisation exists. On any bounded region of the complex plane, however, there exist only finitely many eigenvalues, and we can use CIMs to recover eigenpairs in a domain of interest. All three examples below use the same multi-point Loewner mode. The realisation size \( m \) sits at the largest gap in the singular values of the Loewner matrix \( \mathbb{D} \) (even when the gap is smaller than \( 10^3 \)). A contour whose sample moments are at noise level, below options.EmptyTol \( = 10^{-10} \) relative to their bound, is read as empty, with \( m = 0 \). Eigenvalues with relative residual \( \lVert \mathbf{T}(\lambda)\mathbf{v} \rVert_2 / \lVert \mathbf{T}(\lambda) \rVert_F \geq 10^{-8} \) are drawn as empty grey boxes.

docs.title: 1. A partial element equivalent circuit<sup>1</sup>
docs.text:
A partial element equivalent circuit (PEEC) models a three dimensional circuit interconnect with propagation delay; they are written as delay differential equations. Time-domain solvers are less robust for these equations than for ordinary circuits, so it matters when the model itself is stable2. To this end we consider a test circuit of Bellen, Guglielmi and Ruehli2 given by the neutral delay differential equation

\[ \dot{x}(t) = \mathbf{L}\, x(t) + \mathbf{M}\, x(t-\tau) + \mathbf{N}\, \dot{x}(t-\tau), \qquad x(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}, \]

where the matrices are

\[ \frac{\mathbf{L}}{100} = \begin{pmatrix} -7 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -9 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -6 \end{pmatrix} \quad \frac{\mathbf{M}}{100} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -3 \\ -0.5 & -0.5 & -1 \\ -0.5 & -1.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad \mathbf{N} = \frac{1}{72}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 5 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 3 \\ -2 & 4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \]

Our problem of interest is given as

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda) = \lambda(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{N}e^{-\lambda\tau}) - \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{M}e^{-\lambda\tau}. \]

We can track the eigenvalues of the delay problem as \( \tau \) increases inside, say, an ellipse centred at the origin.

Code (the ellipse CIM and the delay sweep) 
beta = -7;
L = 100*[beta 1 2; 3 -9 0; 1 2 -6];
M = 100*[1 0 -3; -0.5 -0.5 -1; -0.5 -1.5 0];
N = [-1 5 2; 4 0 3; -2 4 1]/72;
I = eye(3);

T = @(s,tau) s*(I - N*exp(-s*tau)) - L - M*exp(-s*tau);
c = Numerics.Contour.Ellipse(0, 2, 10, 1e4);   % semi-axes 2 and 10, 1e4 quadrature nodes

rng(0);
tau = 1;
op  = Numerics.OperatorData(@(s) T(s,tau));
cim = Numerics.CIM(op, c);
cim.RealizationData.ComputationalMode = Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner;
cim.RealizationData.K = 500;  cim.SampleData.ell = 3;  cim.SampleData.r = 3;
% m from the largest singular-value gap of the Loewner matrix; 0 for an empty ellipse
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;

% Each new op.T is sampled on the same contour, with the same probes and shifts.
taus = linspace(0.2, 2, 201);
ews  = cell(size(taus));  rr = cell(size(taus));
for k = 1:numel(taus)
    op.T = @(s) T(s,taus(k));
    [V, D] = cim.eigs();  z = diag(D);
    in = c.inside(z);
    ews{k} = z(in);
    rr{k}  = Numerics.relres(op.T, z(in), V(:,in), op.sample_mode);
end

Plotting code (tau_sweep.png)

The sweep script src/demos/peec/milano_peec_1.m writes ews and their relative residuals rr to peec_tau_sweep.csv, which this script reads.

here = fileparts(mfilename('fullpath'));
S = readtable(fullfile(here, 'peec_tau_sweep.csv'));
tau_ms = 1000*S.tau;
trusted = S.relres < 1e-8;
untrusted = S.relres >= 1e-8;

f = figure('Color', 'w', 'Position', [100 100 500 530]);
hold on;  box on;
th = linspace(0, 2*pi, 400);
plot(2*cos(th), 10*sin(th), 'k-');
xline(0, 'k:');
scatter(S.re(trusted), S.im(trusted), 14, tau_ms(trusted), 'filled');
hu = plot(S.re(untrusted), S.im(untrusted), 's', 'LineStyle', 'none', 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.6 0.6 0.6]);
legend(hu, 'relative residual \geq 10^{-8}', 'Interpreter', 'tex', 'Location', 'northoutside');
colormap(parula);  cb = colorbar;  clim([min(tau_ms) max(tau_ms)]);  cb.Label.String = '\tau [ms]';
xlabel('Re \lambda');  ylabel('Im \lambda');  axis([-2.2 0.6 -10.5 10.5]);

As \( \tau \) grows, eigenvalues enter the ellipse and move toward the imaginary axis. The ellipse holds none at \( \tau = 200 \) ms and 16 at \( \tau = 2000 \) ms. Note that none appear to cross the imaginary axis, and, in fact, this holds for all \( \tau \).

The eigenvalues of \( \mathbf{L} \) are \( -407.9 \) and \( -896 \pm 78i \), so \( \lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{L} \) is invertible for \( \operatorname{Re} \lambda \ge 0 \), and there we can factor

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda) = (\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{L})\big(\mathbf{I} - e^{-\lambda\tau}\mathbf{F}(\lambda)\big), \qquad \mathbf{F}(\lambda) = (\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{L})^{-1}(\lambda\mathbf{N} + \mathbf{M}). \]

The only poles of \( \mathbf{F} \) are the eigenvalues of \( \mathbf{L} \), so \( \mathbf{F} \) is analytic on the closed right half-plane. Further, writing \( \lambda\mathbf{N} = (\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{L})\mathbf{N} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{N} \) gives \( \mathbf{F}(\lambda) = \mathbf{N} + (\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{L})^{-1}(\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{L}\mathbf{N}) \), a stable proper transfer function with \( \mathbf{F}(\lambda) \to \mathbf{N} \) as \( |\lambda| \to \infty \). Its \( \mathcal{H}_\infty \) norm

\[ \|\mathbf{F}\|_{\infty} = \sup_{\operatorname{Re} \lambda \ge 0} \|\mathbf{F}(\lambda)\|_2 = \sup_{\omega \in \mathbb{R}} \|\mathbf{F}(i\omega)\|_2 \]

is finite, and MATLAB computes it from a state-space realisation.

Code (the small-gain bound) 
% T(s) = (sI - L)(I - e^{-s tau} F(s)) with F(s) = N + (sI - L)^{-1}(M + L N).
% L is stable, so ||F||_inf < 1 makes T(s) nonsingular on Re s >= 0 for all tau.
if ~isempty(ver('control')) && license('test', 'Control_Toolbox')
    F = ss(L, M + L*N, eye(3), N);
    fprintf('eig(L) = %s\n', mat2str(eig(L).', 5));
    fprintf('||F||_inf = %.4f\n', hinfnorm(F));
else
    fprintf('Control System Toolbox not available: skipping the H-infinity check.\n');
end

For \( \operatorname{Re} \lambda \ge 0 \) we have \( |e^{-\lambda\tau}| \le 1 \), so \( \|e^{-\lambda\tau}\mathbf{F}(\lambda)\|_2 \le 0.6633 < 1 \). Hence, \( \mathbf{I} - e^{-\lambda\tau}\mathbf{F}(\lambda) \Rightarrow \mathbf{T}(\lambda) \) are nonsingular for every \( \tau \ge 0 \).

Note

ss and hinfnorm require the Control System Toolbox. The rest of this example runs in base MATLAB.

The full demo is src/demos/peec/milano_peec_1.m.

docs.title: 2. A three-bus system with a delayed stabiliser<sup>3</sup>
docs.text:
Wide-area controllers act on remote measurements, so their inputs arrive delayed. Milano's three-bus system3 is a two-machine network whose electromechanical oscillation is damped by a power system stabiliser (PSS); the PSS input is the rotor speed of machine 1, measured with delay \( \tau \). The small-signal model is given as

\[ \dot{x}(t) = \mathbf{A}_0 x(t) + \mathbf{A}_1 x(t - \tau) \]

This is a retarded delay differential equation \( \mathbf{T}(\lambda,\tau)=\lambda\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{A}_0-\mathbf{A}_1 e^{-\lambda\tau} \), with \( \mathbf{A}_0 \) the state matrix of the machines, the automatic voltage regulators (AVRs) and the PSS, and the sparse \( \mathbf{A}_1 \) the delayed speed input of the PSS.

Code (\( \mathbf{A}_0 \), \( \mathbf{A}_1 \) and \( \mathbf{T} \) on 23 states) 
As_base_3bus;   % 19x19 state matrix of Appendix B, without the PSS

Kw = 10.9; Tw = 14; Tz = 0.5056; Tp = 0.1007; gAVR = 40/0.055;
r = Tz/Tp;

% PSS from omega_r1(t - tau) to v_s: x' = Ap x + Bp u, v_s = Cp x + Dp u
Ap = zeros(4); Bp = zeros(4,1);
Ap(1,1) = -1/Tw; Bp(1) = Kw/Tw;
Cp = [-1 0 0 0]; Dp = Kw;
for k = 2:4
    Ap(k,:) = Cp/Tp; Ap(k,k) = Ap(k,k) - 1/Tp; Bp(k) = Dp/Tp;
    Cp = r*Cp; Cp(k) = Cp(k) + (1 - r); Dp = r*Dp;
end

% v_s enters the AVR of machine 1; the delayed omega_r1 enters the PSS
n = 23; iw = 2; iva = 16; ip = 20:23;
E  = eye(n);
A0 = blkdiag(As, Ap); A0(iva,ip) = gAVR*Cp;
A1 = zeros(n); A1(ip,iw) = Bp; A1(iva,iw) = gAVR*Dp;
T  = @(s,tau) s*E - A0 - A1*exp(-s*tau);

One MPLoewner CIM on the circle \( |z - (-0.5 + 4i)| = 2.6 \), with \( K = 50 \) and \( \ell = r = 5 \) fixed probing directions, is reused at 201 delays from 0 to 250 ms.

Code (the CIM, the delay sweep and the margin) 
rng(0);   % the probing directions are drawn once and kept for every delay
c   = Numerics.Contour.Circle(-0.5 + 4i, 2.6, 256);
cim = Numerics.CIM(Numerics.OperatorData(@(s) T(s, 0)), c);
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 50));
cim.SampleData.L = randn(n, 5);  cim.SampleData.R = randn(n, 5);
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;   % m from the largest singular-value gap of the Loewner matrix

tau = linspace(0, 0.25, 201);  sweep = cell(size(tau));
for i = 1:numel(tau)
    sweep{i} = disk_eigs(cim, @(s) T(s, tau(i)));
end

% the first sign change of the abscissa of the trusted eigenvalues on the grid,
% refined by fzero; a disk without trusted eigenvalues reads as stable
tol = 1e-8;   % an eigenvalue with relative residual below tol is trusted
abscissa = @(E) max([real(E.z(E.relres < tol)); -1]);
i  = find(cellfun(abscissa, sweep) > 0, 1);
tc = fzero(@(t) abscissa(disk_eigs(cim, @(s) T(s, t))), tau([i-1 i]));
Ec = disk_eigs(cim, @(s) T(s, tc));  Ec = Ec(Ec.relres < tol, :);
[~, j] = max(real(Ec.z));  zc = Ec.z(j);

function E = disk_eigs(cim, Ttau)
% the eigenvalues z of Ttau inside the contour and their relative residuals
op = cim.SampleData.OperatorData;
op.T = Ttau;   % new samples; the probes and shifts are kept
[V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  z = diag(Lam);
in = cim.SampleData.Contour.inside(z);
E = table(z(in), Numerics.relres(Ttau, z(in), V(:,in), op.sample_mode), 'VariableNames', {'z', 'relres'});
end

Three eigenvalues are recovered inside the contour at every delay, with relative residuals at most \( 7.5\times10^{-19} \). At \( \tau = 50 \) ms they include the delay-critical electromechanical mode near \( -0.75 \pm 5.92i \). Sweeping \( \tau \) drives it across the imaginary axis at the delay margin of 155.3 ms, where it crosses at \( \pm 5.684i \).

Spectrum with and without the PSS Delay-induced instability

The left plot shows the critical portion of the spectrum with and without the PSS. The right plot shows the rightmost eigenvalue in the disk against \( \tau \). The model is built by src/demos/3bus/milano_3bus_ex11_1.m. milano_3bus_spectra.m and milano_3bus_sweep.m in the same folder compute the data, and milano_3bus_figures.m draws both figures from their CSVs.

Sp = Sp(Sp.im >= 0, :);
nop = Sp(Sp.system == "nopss", :);  wp = Sp(Sp.system == "pss", :);

f = figure('Position', [100 100 680 420]);
plot(nop.re, nop.im, 'o', 'MarkerSize', 7, 'LineWidth', 1.2);  hold on;
plot(wp.re, wp.im, '.', 'MarkerSize', 16);
xline(0, 'k-');
xlim([-2.5 0.5]);  ylim([1.5 7]);
xlabel('Re \lambda');  ylabel('Im \lambda');
legend('without PSS', 'with PSS', 'Location', 'northwest');
title('Spectrum with/without PSS');  grid on;

S = readtable(fullfile(here, 'sweep.csv'));
M = readtable(fullfile(here, 'margin.csv'));
tc = M.margin_ms(1);
ok = S.relres < 1e-8;
U = S(~ok, :);  S = S(ok, :);

zs = complex(S.re, S.im);
z = splitapply(@(w) w(find(real(w) == max(real(w)), 1)), zs, g);

f = figure('Position', [100 100 680 380]);
boxstyle = {'s', 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.6 0.6 0.6]};
yyaxis left

if height(U) > 0
    hu = plot(U.tau_ms, U.re, boxstyle{:});
    legend(hu, 'relative residual \geq 10^{-8}', 'Interpreter', 'tex', 'AutoUpdate', 'off');
end

ylabel('Re \lambda');

docs.title: 3. Ten Delayed PSSs on a 39-bus power network<sup>6</sup>
docs.text:
The IEEE PES benchmark version of the New England 39-bus network5 is a published model with ten generators, each with a PSS67. It is given as a differential algebraic equation (DAE)

\[ \dot{x} = f(x,y) \quad | \quad 0 = g(x, y) \]

where \(f\) contains the variables related to generator state, inertia, automatic voltage regulators (AVRs), PSSs, loads, and transmission lines. From the provided Ared.mat, we are given \( A_\text{red} = f_x - f_y g_y^{-1} g_x \), a structured sparse matrix that corresponds to the state of an autonomous LTI system that describes the linearized and reduced DAE. From the state layout of the report's Table 11, we can identify the PSS components explicitly. Without the PSSs the network is unstable, with rightmost eigenvalue \( +0.20 + 5.97i \); with them it is stable, and the rightmost of its oscillatory modes is \( -0.50 + 3.68i \).

Plotting code (pes39_spectra.png)

pes39_spectra.m writes spectra.csv, which this script reads.

here = fileparts(mfilename('fullpath'));
Sp = readtable(fullfile(here, 'spectra.csv'), 'TextType', 'string');
Sp = Sp(Sp.im >= 0, :);
% asinh is linear within about sigma of zero and logarithmic beyond, so the
% electromechanical modes near the axis and the exciter poles near -100 both stay legible
sigma = 0.1;
plog = @(x) asinh(x/(2*sigma))/log(10);
nop = Sp(Sp.system == "nopss", :);  wp = Sp(Sp.system == "pss", :);

f = figure('Position', [100 100 680 420]);
plot(plog(nop.re), nop.im, 'o', 'MarkerSize', 7, 'LineWidth', 1.2);  hold on;
plot(plog(wp.re), wp.im, '.', 'MarkerSize', 16);
xline(0, 'k-');
ticks = [-100 -10 -1 -0.1 0 0.1];
xticks(plog(ticks));  xticklabels(string(ticks));  xlim(plog([-130 0.5]));
xlabel('Re \lambda');  ylabel('Im \lambda');
legend('without PSSs', 'with PSSs', 'Location', 'northwest');
title('Spectrum with/without PSSs');  grid on;

To each identified PSS, we apply a delay, yielding the following retarded problem with ten delays

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda, \tau) = \lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}_0 - \sum_{k=1}^{10} \mathbf{b}_k \mathbf{e}_k^\top e^{-\lambda\tau_k} = \lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A}_0 - \mathbf{B}\operatorname{diag}\big(e^{-\lambda\tau_1}, \dots, e^{-\lambda\tau_{10}}\big)\mathbf{E}^\top, \]

where \( \mathbf{e}_k \) selects the speed of the \( k \)th generator and \( \mathbf{b}_k \) holds \( x_W, x_P, x_Q, E_{fd}, \) and \( x_i \). See the report6 for more details.

Code (\( \mathbf{T}(\lambda, \tau) \) from \( \mathbf{A}_0 \), \( \mathbf{B} \) and \( \mathbf{E} \)) 
% T(tau) is the characteristic matrix for the delay vector tau (10 x 1)
n = size(A0,1);
T = @(tau) @(s) s*eye(n) - A0 - B*diag(exp(-s*tau(:)))*E';

First, we track the rightmost eigenvalue as the common delay \( \tau = \tau_k \) grows, with ten overlapping disks of radius \( \rho = 1 \) centred at \( 3i, 4i, \dots, 12i \). Each disk is an independent CIM computation, so the disks can run in parallel4. A disk returns every eigenvalue it finds inside its contour, and an eigenvalue found by two disks is kept only once via the smaller residual. In the common-delay and single-loop sweeps below, the trusted residuals are at most \( 9.8\times10^{-11} \) in the common-delay sweep.

Code (the disk bank and the trust rule) 
arguments
    Tf
    opts.Centers (1,:) double = 3:12
    opts.Radius (1,1) double = 1
    opts.Nodes (1,1) double = 128
    opts.Mode (1,1) Numerics.ComputationalMode = Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner
    opts.Probes (1,1) double = 5
    opts.K (1,1) double = 50
    opts.Seed (1,1) double = 0
    opts.ResTol (1,1) double = 1e-8
    opts.EmptyTol (1,1) double = 1e-5     % moment level: occupied disks >= 2.5e-3, leakage only <= 1.1e-6
end
% One CIM per disk, all sharing the operator op and the probes L and R. Setting
% op.T resamples every disk; the probes and interpolation points stay. AutoRank
% reads a disk whose moment level is below EmptyTol as empty, and otherwise
% realizes at the largest singular-value gap of its data matrix.
op = Numerics.OperatorData(Tf(zeros(10,1)));
rng(opts.Seed);
L = randn(op.n, opts.Probes);  R = randn(op.n, opts.Probes);
cims = cell(size(opts.Centers));
for k = 1:numel(opts.Centers)
    c = Numerics.Contour.Circle(1i*opts.Centers(k), opts.Radius, opts.Nodes);
    cim = Numerics.CIM(op, c);
    cim.SampleData.L = L;  cim.SampleData.R = R;
    cim.setComputationalMode(opts.Mode, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, opts.K));
    cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;
    cim.options.EmptyTol = opts.EmptyTol;  cim.options.Verbose = false;
    cims{k} = cim;
end

function [ew, res, trusted] = eigenvalues(op, cims, T, restol)
% Every eigenvalue a disk finds inside its contour, with its relative residual
% ||T(z)v|| / ||T(z)||_F.
op.T = T;
ew = zeros(0,1);  res = zeros(0,1);
for k = 1:numel(cims)
    [V, D] = cims{k}.eigs();  z = diag(D);
    in = cims{k}.SampleData.Contour.inside(z);
    ew  = [ew; z(in)];
    res = [res; Numerics.relres(T, z(in), V(:,in), op.sample_mode)];
end
% Overlapping disks find some eigenvalues twice; the copy with the smaller
% residual is kept.
[res, i] = sort(res);  ew = ew(i);
keep = true(size(ew));
for j = 2:numel(ew)
    keep(j) = all(abs(ew(j) - ew(keep(1:j-1))) > 1e-6*max(1, abs(ew(j))));
end
ew = ew(keep);  res = res(keep);
trusted = res < restol;
end
Code (the delay margin) 
function [tc, zc, nb] = pes39_margin(bank, u)
% Delay margin along the delay direction u (10 x 1): the smallest r at which
% the bank of pes39_bank.m trusts an eigenvalue with positive real part at
% tau = r u. Returns Inf when nothing crosses by 500 ms. zc is the rightmost
% trusted eigenvalue at the margin tc, and nb the number of bank evaluations.

% Step outward from 50 ms until the rightmost trusted eigenvalue crosses, then
% refine the crossing with fzero. The bank's fixed probes make the abscissa a
% deterministic function of r.
r = 0.05;  dr = 0.005;  rmax = 0.5;
[a, z] = abscissa(bank, r*u);  nb = 1;
assert(~isnan(z), 'pes39_margin:empty', 'the bank trusts no eigenvalue at tau = %g s', r);
assert(a < 0, 'pes39_margin:start', 'not stable at tau = %g s', r);
while a <= 0
    r = r + dr;
    if r > rmax, tc = Inf;  zc = NaN;  return; end
    a = abscissa(bank, r*u);  nb = nb + 1;
end
[tc, ~, ~, out] = fzero(@(x) abscissa(bank, x*u), [r - dr, r]);
[~, zc] = abscissa(bank, tc*u);
nb = nb + out.funcCount + 1;
end

function [a, z] = abscissa(bank, tau)
% The rightmost trusted eigenvalue z in the bank at the delays tau and its real
% part a; a = -1 and z = NaN when the bank trusts none.
[ew, ~, trusted] = bank(tau);
ew = ew(trusted);
if isempty(ew), a = -1;  z = NaN;  return; end
[a, i] = max(real(ew));  z = ew(i);
end
Code (the common-delay sweep) 
bank = pes39_bank(Tf);  one = ones(10,1);
cols = {'tau_ms', 're', 'im', 'res', 'trusted'};
tau = linspace(0, 0.15, 201);  sweep = cell(numel(tau), 1);
for j = 1:numel(tau)
    [ew, res, trusted] = bank(tau(j)*one);
    sweep{j} = table(repmat(1e3*tau(j), numel(ew), 1), real(ew), imag(ew), res, trusted, 'VariableNames', cols);
end

We find that the stability margin of the entire system is \( \sim 96 \) ms. The rightmost eigenvalue switches from \( 3.81i \) to \( 10.49i \) between 63.75 and 64.50 ms, and again, from \( 10.18i \) to \( 10.62i \), at about 114 ms. The left CIM bank figure below shows trajectories as the common delay grows from \( 0 - 150 \) ms.

Next, we examine the effect of a delay on a single PSS, as if it had a sudden drop in a speed signal; we take \( \tau = \tau_k \mathbf{e}_k \) for \( k = 1, \ldots, 10 \), while the other nine act without delay. The table below shows the delayed PSS, its rightmost eigenvalue at the stability margin, and the corresponding delay. Note that the PSS on generators 1 and 10 with individual delays did not make the system unstable up to a delay of 500 ms. The right CIM bank figure shows the eigenvalue trajectory associated with the delay associated with the worst case, generator 4.

Rightmost \( \operatorname{Re}\lambda \) against the common delay

Delay margin with a single delayed PSS

Generator Rightmost eigenvalue at the margin Delay margin [ms] 1 --- --- 2 \( 7.675i \) 178.32 3 \( 8.845i \) 114.35 4 \( 10.222i \) 101.06 5 \( 7.001i \) 250.56 6 \( 8.673i \) 252.49 7 \( 10.552i \) 157.11 8 \( 10.828i \) 101.30 9 \( 8.257i \) 114.33 10 --- --- The disk bank as the common delay grows The disk bank as \( \tau_4 \) grows

The model is built by src/demos/pes39/pes39_model.m. In the same folder, pes39_spectra.m, pes39_common_margin.m, pes39_single_margin.m, pes39_sweep.m and pes39_single_sweep.m compute the data, and pes39_figures.m draws the four figures from their CSVs.

  2. A. Bellen, N. Guglielmi, and A. E. Ruehli, "Methods for Linear Systems of Circuit Delay Differential Equations of Neutral Type," IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Fundamental Theory and Applications, vol. 46, no. 1, pp. 212-216, 1999. ↩↩

  3. Milano, Dassios, Liu, and, Tzounas, Eigenvalue Problems in Power Systems. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, 2020. The three-bus system is defined in Appendix A, A_S is given in Appendix B; the delayed-PSS study is Example 11.1, and the PSS design is Example 4.3. ↩↩

  4. S. Gao, Z. Du, and Y. Li, "Estimating Number of Critical Eigenvalues of Large-Scale Power System Based on Contour Integral," IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, vol. 36, no. 6, pp. 5854-5862, 2021, doi: 10.1109/TPWRS.2021.3084683. ↩

docs.title: The Gun Problem: a Large and Sparse Benchmark
docs.text:
The gun problem1 models the resonances of a radio-frequency gun cavity and is a standard large-scale benchmark of the nonlinear-eigenvalue literature. We consider the operator given as

\[ \mathbf{T}(\lambda) \;=\; \mathbf{K} \;-\; \lambda\mathbf{M} \;+\; i\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathbf{E}_1 \;+\; i\sqrt{\lambda-\sigma_2^2}\,\mathbf{E}_2, \qquad \sigma_2 = 108.8774, \]

with all four coefficient matrices sparse \( 9956\times9956 \) matrices from a finite-element discretisation. The square roots make the problem genuinely nonlinear. Due to the problem size, a dense sampler would be prohibitively expensive, so, in CIMTOOL, we take advantage of the sparsity of \( \mathbf{T}(z) \) where possible. Additional computation efficiencies can be derived if more structure is known about the underlying operator.

Brennan, Embree and Gugercin2 compare the Hankel, single-point Loewner and multipoint Loewner methods, on the disk \( |\lambda - 141000| < 30000 \), which holds \( m = 17 \) eigenvalues; we repeat a similar experiment with CIMTOOL, opting to use separate left and right shift sets.

Each method realizes 17 eigenvalues from \( 32\times32 \) data matrices, built from \( K \) moments or interpolation points and \( \ell = r \) probing directions such that \( K \ell = 32 \). The single-point Loewner shift is \( \sigma = 141000 - 40000i \), directly below the contour. Multipoint Loewner places \( K \) right points \( \sigma_j \) on the concentric circle of radius 40000, starting at \( 141000 + 40000i \), and \( K \) left points \( \theta_i \) midway between them, so that the shift sets are interleaved.

When switching computational modes and \( K/m \) parameters, we do not need to resample \( T^{-1} \); all three methods use the same sample set. The demo samples \( \mathbf{T}(z)^{-1}\mathbf{R} \) and \( \mathbf{L}^*\mathbf{T}(z)^{-1} \) for 16 directions on nested trapezoid rules with \( N = 16, 32, \ldots, 1024 \). Each case then utilizes only the leading \( \ell \) directions to realize \( H \).

We compute the maximum relative residual \( \max_j \lVert \mathbf{T}(\lambda_j)\mathbf{v}_j\rVert_2 / \lVert \mathbf{T}(\lambda_j)\rVert_F \) over the 17 computed eigenpairs. The figure below shows how different numbers of moments/probing can affect performance of the three modes.

\( (K, r) \) Hankel single-point Loewner multipoint Loewner \( (2, 16) \) \( 8.7\times10^{-9} \) \( 6.2\times10^{-16} \) \( 3.1\times10^{-17} \) \( (4, 8) \) \( 3.2\times10^{-4} \) \( 3.6\times10^{-4} \) \( 5.7\times10^{-17} \) \( (8, 4) \) \( 3.6\times10^{-4} \) \( 3.4\times10^{-4} \) \( 9.6\times10^{-16} \)

The figure shows the contour and shift placement, as well as maximum relative residuals and the singular value decay of the three modes for each of the three cases we consider. The table gives the residuals of the three modes at \( N = 1024 \). With 16 directions both SP/MPLoewner converge to machine precision, while Hankel stalls at \( \sim 10^{-8} \). With 4 or 8 directions, Hankel and SPLoewner stall at \( \sim 3\times10^{-4} \) for every \( N >= 64 \), and MPLoewner still converges.

The demo is src/demos/gun/gun_nlevp.m, and src/demos/gun/gun_figures.m draws the figure from its CSVs. The NLEVP collection is required to be on the MATLAB path.

Tisseur, "NLEVP: A Collection of Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problems," ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, vol. 39, no. 2, 2013, doi: 10.1145/2427023.2427024. The gun problem originates in B.-S. Liao, Z. Bai, L.-Q. Lee, and K. Ko, "Nonlinear Rayleigh-Ritz iterative method for solving large scale nonlinear eigenvalue problems," Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics, vol. 14, no. 3A, pp. 869-883, 2010. ↩

  2. M. C. Brennan, M. Embree, and S. Gugercin, "Contour Integral Methods for Nonlinear Eigenvalue Problems: A Systems Theoretic Approach," SIAM Review, vol. 65, no. 2, pp. 439-470, 2023, doi: 10.1137/20M1389303. -- (Fig. 7, Sec. 5.4) ↩

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: In the acoustic-wave-1D example the operator was a matrix polynomial in \( \lambda \), obtained by discretising a 1-D Helmholtz equation. Discretisation captures low-frequency eigenmodes of the underlying infinite-dimensional problem well, but degrades for high-frequency modes. This suggests working with the infinite-dimensional problem directly, trading polynomial nonlinearities for more general, transcendental ones.

docs.title: Plane Wave Solutions of the 1-D Wave Equation
docs.text:
Consider the 1-D wave equation

\[ u_{tt}(x,t) = c^2 u_{xx}(x,t), \quad x \in [0,1], \quad t > 0, \]

with boundary conditions

\[ u(0,t) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad u(1,t) = u_x(1,t), \quad t > 0. \]

The ansatz \( u(x,t) = f(x) e^{i\lambda t} \), \( \lambda \in \mathbb{C} \), gives

\[ f_{xx}(x) = - \left( \frac{\lambda}{c} \right)^2 f(x). \]

Fixing \( c = 1 \), the function \( f(x) = \sin{( \lambda x )} \) satisfies the equation, and the right-hand boundary condition then requires

\[ \sin{ \lambda } = \lambda \cos{ \lambda } \;\Leftrightarrow\; T(\lambda) \coloneqq \tan{ \lambda } - \lambda = 0. \]

\( T(\lambda) = 0 \) is a scalar transcendental eigenvalue problem. Each root gives an exact eigenmode \( f(x) \) of the continuous problem.

Finding eigenvalues of \(T\) 
T = @(s) tan(s) - s;

tol = 10^-6; Ni = 2000; x = linspace(0,20,Ni); ew = zeros(size(x));
for i = 1:length(x)
    ew(i) = fzero(T,x(i));
end
ew = ew(ew > 2); ew = ew(abs(T(ew)) < tol); ew = uniquetol(ew,sqrt(tol));
Eigenvalues/Poles of \(T\) First 5 eigenmodes Plotting code (pzT.png, f5ms.png)

Continues from the eigenvalue sweep above (ew).

% T(lambda) with its eigenvalues (dots) and poles (dashed)
poles = (0.5:1:6.5)*pi;  poles = poles(poles <= 20);
xg = linspace(0,20,4000);  yg = tan(xg) - xg;
yg(abs(diff([yg yg(end)])) > 50) = NaN;          % break the curve across poles
f = figure('Position',[100 100 700 525],'Color','w');  hold on
plot(xg, yg, 'b-', 'LineWidth', 1);
for p = poles;  hP = xline(p, 'r--', 'LineWidth', 1);  end
hZ = plot(ew, zeros(size(ew)), 'k.', 'MarkerSize', 22);
hold off;  ylim([-25 25]);  xlim([0 20]);
xlabel('\lambda');  ylabel('T(\lambda) = tan\lambda - \lambda');
legend([hZ hP], {'eigenvalues','poles'}, 'Location','northoutside', ...
    'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off');

% the first five eigenmodes f(x) = sin(lambda x)
lam5 = ew(1:5);  xf = linspace(0,1,400);  lbl = strings(1,5);
f = figure('Position',[100 100 700 525],'Color','w');  hold on
for k = 1:5
    plot(xf, sin(lam5(k)*xf), 'LineWidth', 1.5);
    lbl(k) = sprintf('\\lambda_%d = %.4f', k, lam5(k));
end
hold off;  ylim([-1 1]);  xlim([0 1]);
xlabel('x');  ylabel('f(x) = sin(\lambda x)');
legend(lbl, 'Location','northoutside', 'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off');

A single string gives a scalar problem. The same construction on a network of strings produces matrix-valued transcendental problems, some of whose eigenvalues are available in closed form.

docs.title: Networks of Strings
docs.text:
The nlevp_webs project2 assembles the planar modal vibrations of any network of elastic strings into an NLEVP. On each string's interior the wave equation is solved exactly by sines and cosines, and the eigenvalue enters only through the boundary and junction conditions. The construction converts a linear, infinite-dimensional problem into a nonlinear, finite-dimensional one3.

On string \( i \), component \( j \) of the modal displacement is a standing wave with sine coefficient \( A_{i,j} \) and cosine coefficient \( B_{i,j} \), where \( j = 1 \) is the longitudinal direction and \( j \ge 2 \) are transverse. The coefficients are constrained by the fixed-frame condition at anchored ends, and by continuity and force balance at each free node. The full construction goes into more detail2. Note that eigenvalues with relative residual \( \lVert T(\lambda)\mathbf{v} \rVert_2 / \lVert T(\lambda) \rVert_F \geq 10^{-8} \) are marked with empty grey boxes in the figures below.

docs.title: The Three-String ("Tritare")
docs.text:
The tritare1 is the simplest interesting case: three strings meeting at a single free junction and anchored to the frame at their outer ends (\( n_e = 3 \)), vibrating in the plane (\( D = 2 \)). tritare.m gives reference eigenvalues computed to 30 digits for two arm angles \( \theta \in \{\pi/2,\, 2\pi/3\} \). \( \theta \) is the angle between two of the string arms, with the third string, lying opposite the arm bisector. We consider \( \theta = \pi/2 \) first, with all eigenvalues purely imaginary (\( \lambda = i\omega \), no damping). On a circle enclosing the ten lowest-frequency eigenvalues, CIM determines the enclosed count from the numerical rank of the Loewner data matrix. It returns all 10 eigenvalues to machine precision (see src/demos/webs/tritare_web.m).

Code 
[T, TV, gamma, nodes, edges, ew_ref] = tritare(pi/2);   % 12x12, references to 30 digits

op  = Numerics.OperatorData(T);
c   = Numerics.Contour.Circle(2i, 1.5, 512);
cim = Numerics.CIM(op, c);
cim.SampleData.ell = 12;  cim.SampleData.r = 12;
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 64));
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;   % m at the largest gap in the singular values of the Loewner matrix

[V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  ew = diag(Lam);
in = c.inside(ew);  ew = ew(in);  V = V(:,in);
res = Numerics.relres(T, ew, V, op.sample_mode);
ok  = res < 1e-8;                      % trusted eigenpairs
fprintf('%d enclosed / %d recovered, %d trusted (rank %d), matching distance %.1e, max relres %.1e\n', ...
    nnz(c.inside(ew_ref)), numel(ew), nnz(ok), cim.ResultData.m, Numerics.matching_distance(ew_ref, ew), max(res));

The eigenvector \( \mathbf{v} \) holds the coefficients \( A_{i,j}, B_{i,j} \) of the mode shape, so it can be plotted directly as a vibrating Y:

Recovered vs 30-digit reference Mode shape from the CIM eigenvector (\( \omega_3 \approx 1.55994 \))

The right panel reconstructs the third mode from its CIM eigenvector via the nlevp_webs mode_curves (grey: strings at rest; black: the displaced web).

Plotting code (tritare_eigs.png, tritare_mode.png)

Continues from the block above (c, ew, V, ok, ew_ref, and the geometry TV, gamma, nodes, edges).

% trusted eigenvalues (dots), untrusted ones (grey squares), 30-digit references (circles) and the contour
f = figure('Position',[100 100 700 525],'Color','w');  hold on
h = [plot([c.z c.z(1)], 'k-', 'LineWidth', 1), ...
     plot(real(ew_ref), imag(ew_ref), 'ko', 'MarkerSize', 9, 'LineWidth', 1), ...
     plot(real(ew(ok)), imag(ew(ok)), 'b.', 'MarkerSize', 20)];
lbl = {'contour','reference','CIM'};
if any(~ok)
    h(end+1) = plot(real(ew(~ok)), imag(ew(~ok)), 's', 'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.6 0.6 0.6], 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerSize', 7);
    lbl{end+1} = 'relative residual \geq 10^{-8}';
end
hold off;  axis equal;  xlim([-3 3]);  ylim([-0.2 8.2]);
xlabel('Re \lambda');  ylabel('Im \lambda');
legend(h, lbl, 'Location','northoutside', 'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off');

% the mode shape of the third eigenpair (omega_3 = 1.55994) via mode_curves
v = V(:,3);  [~, ip] = max(abs(v));  v = real(v / exp(1i*angle(v(ip))));   % rotate to a real vector
R = real(mode_curves(ew(3), v, TV, gamma, nodes, edges, 1, 0, 0.3, 60));
f = figure('Position',[100 100 700 525],'Color','w');  hold on
plot([nodes(edges(:,1),1)' ; nodes(edges(:,2),1)'], ...
     [nodes(edges(:,1),2)' ; nodes(edges(:,2),2)'], '-', 'Color', [0.7 0.7 0.7]);
for i = 1:size(R,3)
    plot(R(1,:,i), R(2,:,i), 'k.-', 'MarkerSize', 16, 'MarkerIndices', 1:3:60);
end
hold off;  axis off;  axis equal;

docs.title: Classifying Eigenvalue Types on the Symmetric Tritare
docs.text:
At \( \theta = 2\pi/3 \) the tritare becomes a symmetric three-armed star. Symmetry makes the whole spectrum solvable in closed form, which gives an exact reference for what CIMTOLL reads off of a contour. The assembled operator \( T(\lambda) \) is \( 2Dn_e \times 2Dn_e = 12\times12 \), one column per coefficient \( A_{i,j}, B_{i,j} \)2. Every string is anchored to the frame at one end, so \( B_{i,j} = 0 \) for all \( i, j \); what remains is an order-6 problem in the sine coefficients. It is written for real \( \omega \), with \( \lambda = i\omega \), and denoted \( \widehat T \) to separate it from the \( 12\times12 \) operator:

\[ \widehat T(\omega)\begin{pmatrix}A_{1,1}\\A_{1,2}\\A_{2,1}\\A_{2,2}\\A_{3,1}\\A_{3,2}\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{0},\qquad \widehat T(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix} \sin\sqrt2\omega & 0 & \tfrac12\sin\sqrt2\omega & -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin2\omega & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \sin2\omega & \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin\sqrt2\omega & \tfrac12\sin2\omega & 0 & 0\\ \sin\sqrt2\omega & 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac12\sin\sqrt2\omega & -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin2\omega\\ 0 & \sin2\omega & 0 & 0 & -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin\sqrt2\omega & -\tfrac12\sin2\omega\\ \sqrt2\cos\sqrt2\omega & 0 & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cos\sqrt2\omega & \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos2\omega & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\cos\sqrt2\omega & \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos2\omega\\ 0 & \cos2\omega & -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}\cos\sqrt2\omega & -\tfrac12\cos2\omega & \tfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}\cos\sqrt2\omega & \tfrac12\cos2\omega \end{pmatrix}. \]

The top four rows are the continuity conditions at the junction, and the bottom two are the force-balance condition. The longitudinal and transverse phases across a string are \( \sqrt2\,\omega \) and \( 2\omega \). general_web assembles the same conditions up to row scaling and the orientation of each string's local axes, so the eigenvalues agree.

The eigenvalues fall into three types3, which follow from examining how the four continuity rows can vanish.

Type Condition Frequencies 1 (transverse) \( \sin 2\omega = 0 \) \( \omega = m\pi/2 \) 2 (longitudinal) \( \sin\sqrt2\,\omega = 0 \) \( \omega = m\pi/\sqrt2 \) 3 (junction-moving) \( \tan\sqrt2\,\omega + \sqrt2\tan 2\omega = 0 \) transcendental

The figure below shows one mode shape per type: the junction fixed with arms bowing (type 1), the junction fixed with longitudinal compression visible in the dot spacing (type 2), and the whole web swinging about a displaced junction (type 3).

Plotting code (tritare_types.png)

Recovers one trusted representative of each family and reconstructs its mode shape with mode_curves.

% one trusted eigenvector of each type, each from a small circle around its frequency
[T, TV, gamma, nodes, edges, ew_ref] = tritare(2*pi/3);
wl = [pi/2, pi/sqrt(2), imag(ew_ref(1))];          % type 1, 2, 3 representatives
opt  = Numerics.OperatorData(T);
ct   = Numerics.Contour.Circle(1i*wl(1), 0.08, 256);
cimt = Numerics.CIM(opt, ct);
cimt.SampleData.ell = 8;  cimt.SampleData.r = 8;
cimt.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 64));
cimt.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;
modeV = cell(1,3);
for t = 1:3
    ct.gamma = 1i*wl(t);                           % the shifts follow the circle, the probes stay
    [V, Lam] = cimt.eigs();  z = diag(Lam);
    ok = ct.inside(z) & Numerics.relres(T, z, V, opt.sample_mode) < 1e-8;
    v = V(:, find(ok, 1));
    [~, ip] = max(abs(v));  modeV{t} = real(v / exp(1i*angle(v(ip))));
end

ttl = {'Type 1: transverse  (\omega = \pi/2)', ...
       'Type 2: longitudinal  (\omega = \pi/\surd2)', ...
       'Type 3: junction-moving  (\omega \approx 0.947)'};
scl = [0.30 0.60 0.30];                            % longitudinal needs a larger scale to read
f = figure('Position',[100 100 1200 420],'Color','w');
tiledlayout(1,3,'Padding','compact','TileSpacing','compact');
for t = 1:3
    nexttile;  hold on
    R = real(mode_curves(1i*wl(t), modeV{t}, TV, gamma, nodes, edges, 1, 0, scl(t), 80));
    plot([nodes(edges(:,1),1)' ; nodes(edges(:,2),1)'], ...
         [nodes(edges(:,1),2)' ; nodes(edges(:,2),2)'], '-', 'Color', [0.72 0.72 0.72], 'LineWidth', 1);
    for i = 1:size(R,3)
        plot(R(1,:,i), R(2,:,i), 'k.-', 'MarkerSize', 9, 'LineWidth', 1);
    end
    plot(0, 0, 'ko', 'MarkerSize', 5, 'MarkerFaceColor', 'k');   % the junction
    hold off;  axis equal;  axis off;  title(ttl{t});
end

For type 1 eigenvalues the tritare rings as three individual strings clamped at each end (the endpoints and the shared junction). The longitudinal coefficients \( A_{i,1} \) vanish and the eigenvector is a multiple of \( [0,1,0,1,0,-1]^\top \). Type 2 forces \( A_{i,2} = 0 \), and the eigenvector is a multiple of \( [1,0,1,0,1,0]^\top \). For type 3 the junction moves, and the eigenspace is two-dimensional:

\[ \operatorname{span}\left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 2\sin\sqrt2\omega \\ -\sqrt3\,\sin2\omega \\ -\sin\sqrt2\omega \\ \sqrt3\,\sin2\omega \\ \sin\sqrt2\omega \end{pmatrix},\; \begin{pmatrix} 2\sin2\omega \\ 0 \\ -\sin2\omega \\ \sqrt3\,\sin\sqrt2\omega \\ -\sin2\omega \\ \sqrt3\,\sin\sqrt2\omega \end{pmatrix} \right\}. \]

Of the 24 reference eigenvalues, 5 are of type 1, 3 of type 2, and 16 of type 3 (eight distinct values, each a derogatory double).

docs.title: Realizing Eigenpairs
docs.text:
The derogatory doubles, linearly dependent eigenvectors of the type-1 and type-2 families, and closed-form reference make the symmetric three-string a great validation problem for CIM solvers3. The contour of the \( \theta = \pi/2 \) example, \( \texttt{Circle(2i, 1.5)} \), is reused on the \( \theta = 2\pi/3 \) operator. It encloses nine eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, six of them the three type-3 doubles. The count is one lower than at \( \theta = \pi/2 \) because one eigenvalue leaves the circle at \( \theta \approx 1.72 \).

The left panel colours each recovered eigenvalue by family, while the right panel shows the principal subspace angle between each recovered eigenvector and the analytic eigenspace.

Code (eigenvalue and eigenvector accuracy)

Continues from the \( \theta = \pi/2 \) block above, whose CIM (op, c, cim) is reused.

% the theta = pi/2 CIM, with its contour and probes, on the symmetric operator
[T, ~, ~, ~, ~, ew_ref] = tritare(2*pi/3);
op.T = T;
[V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  ew = diag(Lam);
in = c.inside(ew);  ew = ew(in);  V = V(:,in);
ok = Numerics.relres(T, ew, V, op.sample_mode) < 1e-8;   % trusted eigenpairs

% eigenvalue error, and subspace angle to the analytic eigenspace at the nearest reference
ang = zeros(numel(ew),1);  eer = zeros(numel(ew),1);  jref = zeros(numel(ew),1);
for i = 1:numel(ew)
    [eer(i), jref(i)] = min(abs(ew(i) - ew_ref));
    ang(i) = subspace(V(:,i), null(T(ew_ref(jref(i)))));
end
fprintf('Loewner rank %d, %d eigenvalues, %d trusted; max eigenvalue error %.1e, max eigenvector angle %.1e\n', ...
    cim.ResultData.m, numel(ew), nnz(ok), max(eer), max(ang));

% each double: the recovered pair must span the two-dimensional null space, not just lie in it
for j = unique(jref).'
    pr = find(jref == j);
    if numel(pr) == 2
        N = null(T(ew_ref(j)));
        fprintf('double at %.6fi: pair rank %d, angle between recovered and analytic 2-spaces %.1e\n', ...
            imag(ew_ref(j)), rank(V(:,pr), 1e-8), subspace(V(:,pr), N));
    end
end
Plotting code (tritare_recovery.png)

Continues from the block above (c, ew, ew_ref, ang, ok); colours each eigenvalue by its family.

cls = zeros(numel(ew),1);                           % the type of each recovered eigenvalue
for i = 1:numel(ew)
    ww = imag(ew(i));
    if abs(sin(2*ww)) < 1e-4, cls(i)=1; elseif abs(sin(sqrt(2)*ww)) < 1e-4, cls(i)=2; else cls(i)=3; end
end
cls(~ok) = 4;                                       % untrusted, whatever its type
col = [0.00 0.45 0.74; 0.20 0.60 0.20; 0.85 0.15 0.15; 0.6 0.6 0.6];
mk  = {'.', '.', '.', 's'};  msl = [30 30 30 7];  msr = [26 26 26 7];   % marker sizes, left and right panel
tn  = {'type 1 (transverse)','type 2 (longitudinal)','type 3 (derogatory)','relative residual \geq 10^{-8}'};
f = figure('Position',[100 100 1180 470],'Color','w');
tiledlayout(1,2,'Padding','compact','TileSpacing','loose');

nexttile;  hold on                                 % left: recovered spectrum by type
hC = plot([c.z c.z(1)], 'k-', 'LineWidth', 1);
hR = plot(real(ew_ref), imag(ew_ref), 'o', 'Color',[0.6 0.6 0.6], 'MarkerSize',11, 'LineWidth',1);
h = NaN(1,4);
for i = 1:numel(ew)
    h(cls(i)) = plot(real(ew(i)), imag(ew(i)), mk{cls(i)}, 'MarkerEdgeColor', col(cls(i),:), 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerSize', msl(cls(i)));
end
hold off;  axis equal;  xlim([-1.7 1.7]);  ylim([-0.2 8.2]);
xlabel('Re \lambda');  ylabel('Im \lambda');  title('recovered spectrum');
lg = [hC hR];  lgs = {'contour','reference'};
for k = 1:4, if ~isnan(h(k)), lg=[lg h(k)]; lgs=[lgs tn(k)]; end, end
legend(lg, lgs, 'Location','northoutside', 'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off', 'NumColumns',3);

nexttile;  hold on                                 % right: eigenvector subspace angle
for i = 1:numel(ew)
    stem(imag(ew(i)), max(ang(i),1e-17), 'Color', col(cls(i),:), 'Marker','none', 'LineWidth',1.2);
    plot(imag(ew(i)), max(ang(i),1e-17), mk{cls(i)}, 'MarkerEdgeColor', col(cls(i),:), 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerSize', msr(cls(i)));
end
yline(eps, 'k:', '\epsilon_{mach}', 'Color',[0.4 0.4 0.4]);
hold off;  set(gca,'YScale','log');  ylim([1e-17 1e0]);  xlim([0.5 3.5]);
xlabel('\omega = Im \lambda');  ylabel('subspace angle to analytic eigenvector (rad)');
title('eigenvector accuracy');

docs.title: \( \theta \) as a parameter
docs.text:
tritare(θ) assembles \( T(\lambda;\theta) \) for any \( \theta \in (0,\pi) \), so the \( \theta = \pi/2 \) and \( \theta = 2\pi/3 \) problems above are two slices of a single parametric NLEVP2. The figure traces the eigenvalues within the same circle as the previous section as \( \theta \) sweeps \( [\pi/6, 5\pi/6] \):

At \( \theta = 2\pi/3 \) the type-3 frequencies are doubles (circled), where eigenvalues cross. Changing the angle away from \( 2 \pi / 3 \) breaks the symmetry and splits each double into two simple eigenvalues; type-1 and type-2 frequencies stay simple.

Code (eigenvalue trajectories vs \( \theta \))

Continues from the blocks above, reusing the \( \theta = \pi/2 \) CIM at every arm angle.

% the theta = pi/2 CIM on Circle(2i, 1.5), at every arm angle
th = linspace(pi/6, 5*pi/6, 201);
loci = cell(size(th));  rr = cell(size(th));       % the frequencies inside, and their relative residuals
for k = 1:numel(th)
    op.T = tritare(th(k));
    [V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  z = diag(Lam);  in = c.inside(z);
    loci{k} = imag(z(in));
    rr{k} = Numerics.relres(op.T, z(in), V(:,in), op.sample_mode);
end
ok = vertcat(rr{:}) < 1e-8;                        % trusted eigenpairs
fprintf('theta sweep: %d eigenvalues inside at %d angles, %d trusted, %d untrusted (max relres %.1e)\n', ...
    numel(ok), numel(th), nnz(ok), nnz(~ok), max(vertcat(rr{:})));
Plotting code (tritare_loci.png)

Continues from the loop above (c, th, loci, ok); shades the enclosed band and marks the two example slices.

[~, k3] = min(abs(th - 2*pi/3));
d3 = loci{k3}(diff(loci{k3}) < 1e-6);             % the type-3 doubles at theta = 2*pi/3
TH = repelem(th, cellfun(@numel, loci));  OM = vertcat(loci{:});
band = imag(c.gamma) + [-1 1]*c.rho;              % the frequencies inside the circle
f = figure('Position',[100 100 780 600],'Color','w');  hold on
hB = patch([pi/6 5*pi/6 5*pi/6 pi/6], band([1 1 2 2]), [0.85 0.90 0.97], 'EdgeColor','none', 'FaceAlpha',0.7);
h = [plot(TH(ok), OM(ok), '.', 'Color',[0.15 0.15 0.15], 'MarkerSize', 5), hB, ...
     xline(pi/2,   'b--', 'LineWidth', 1), ...
     xline(2*pi/3, 'r--', 'LineWidth', 1), ...
     plot(2*pi/3*ones(size(d3)), d3, 'ro', 'MarkerSize', 9, 'LineWidth', 1.4)];
lbl = {'eigenvalues', 'inside Circle(2i, 1.5)', ...
    '\theta = \pi/2 (first example)', '\theta = 2\pi/3 (symmetric tritare)', 'type-3 doubles'};
if any(~ok)
    h(end+1) = plot(TH(~ok), OM(~ok), 's', 'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.6 0.6 0.6], 'MarkerFaceColor', 'none', 'MarkerSize', 7);
    lbl{end+1} = 'relative residual \geq 10^{-8}';
end
plot([pi/6 5*pi/6], band([2 2]), 'k-', 'LineWidth', 0.5);
hold off;  xlim([pi/6 5*pi/6]);  ylim([0 4]);
xticks((1:5)*pi/6);  xticklabels({'\pi/6','\pi/3','\pi/2','2\pi/3','5\pi/6'});
xlabel('arm angle  \theta  (radians)');  ylabel('\omega = Im \lambda');
title('eigenvalue trajectories as a function of \theta');
legend(h, lbl, 'Location','northoutside', 'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off', 'NumColumns',3);

docs.title: The \(n\)-string and Loewner Probing
docs.text:
The eigenvalue types generalize as \(n\) is varied. general_web builds the \( n \)-armed star directly, with unit tensions balanced at the junction for any \( n \). Each of the \( n \) arms carries an independent transverse clamped-string mode at \( \omega = \pi/2 \), and force balance at the junction removes two of the \( n \) arm amplitudes. Thus, the type-1 eigenvalue at \( i\pi/2 \) has multiplicity \( n - 2 \)3.

Code 
% the n-armed star: n strings of length 2 from a junction at the origin, 4n x 4n
phi  = @(n) 2*pi*(0:n-1)'/n;
star = @(n) general_web([0 0; 2*cos(phi(n)) 2*sin(phi(n))], [(2:n+1)' ones(n,1)], 1, 1, 2, 0);

op  = Numerics.OperatorData(star(3));
c   = Numerics.Contour.Circle(1i*pi/2, 0.1, 256);
cim = Numerics.CIM(op, c);
cim.SampleData.ell = 8;  cim.SampleData.r = 8;
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 64));
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;

svals = cell(1,6);                                  % the Loewner singular values, for the plot
for n = 3:6
    op.T = star(n);                                 % a new size draws new probes
    [V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  ew = diag(Lam);
    in = c.inside(ew);  ew = ew(in);  V = V(:,in);
    svals{n} = diag(cim.ResultData.Sigma) / cim.ResultData.Sigma(1);
    res = Numerics.relres(op.T, ew, V, op.sample_mode);
    fprintf('n=%d (T is %2dx%2d): rank %d = n-2, %d trusted, dist to i*pi/2 %.1e, max relres %.1e\n', ...
        n, 4*n, 4*n, cim.ResultData.m, nnz(res < 1e-8), max(abs(ew - 1i*pi/2)), max(res));
end

Plotting code (nstar_mult.png)

Continues from the loop above (svals).

f = figure('Position',[100 100 700 525],'Color','w');  hold on
lbl = strings(1,4);
for n = 3:6
    kk = 1:min(10, numel(svals{n}));
    semilogy(kk, svals{n}(kk), 'o-', 'LineWidth', 1.2, 'MarkerSize', 6);
    lbl(n-2) = sprintf('n = %d  (mult %d)', n, n-2);
end
hold off;  set(gca,'YScale','log');  ylim([1e-16 2]);  xlim([1 10]);
xlabel('index k');  ylabel('\sigma_k / \sigma_1');
legend(lbl, 'Location','northoutside', 'Orientation','horizontal', 'Box','off');

The number of probing directions bounds the recoverable multiplicity

The one-sided samples \( \mathbf{L}^*\mathbf{T}(z)^{-1} \) and \( \mathbf{T}(z)^{-1}\mathbf{R} \) can expose an eigenspace of dimension at most \( \min(\ell, r) \). Rerunning the \( n = 6 \) star with \( \ell = r = 2 \) undercounts the multiplicity-4 eigenvalue:

% the n = 6 star of the loop above, realized from two of its probes per side
cim.SampleData.ell = 2;  cim.SampleData.r = 2;
cim.compute();
fprintf('n=6 with ell = r = 2: Loewner rank %d (true multiplicity 4)\n', cim.ResultData.m);

The realized eigenvalue undercounts the true multiplicity, and the Loewner singular values do not indicate this. When multiple eigenvalues are possible, \( \ell \) and \( r \) should be at least as large as the maximum multiplicity to be resolved. §4.2.2 of 2 bounds the number of moments needed for a full-rank realization through the Cayley–Hamilton theorem and the degree of the minimal polynomial. Its Theorem 4.2 caps the rank gained per moment within a left-invariant subspace at the rank of the probing directions restricted to it.

docs.title: A Large-Scale Orb-Weaver's Web
docs.text:
The runnable companion is at src/demos/webs/orb_web.m.

nlevp_webs' spider2 is a traced orb-weaver web with 633 nodes and 1241 string edges, whose planar modal vibrations give a \( 4964 \times 4964 \) trigonometric NEP. general_web assembles \( T(\lambda) \) densely, but the operator is sparse (0.16 % dense). CIMTOOL can take advantage of this by using sparse solves at each quadrature point, saving a substantial amount of memory (a dense \( n \times n \times K \) sample array at \( K = 48 \) would be \(\approx\)19 GB).

Code 
[Td, TV, gam, nodes, edges, ew_ref] = spider2();
T = @(s) sparse(Td(s));                            % assembled dense, but string-local: sample it sparse

op  = Numerics.OperatorData(T);
c   = Numerics.Contour.Circle(0.0278i, 0.005, 128);   % encloses the two lowest modes
cim = Numerics.CIM(op, c);
cim.SampleData.ell = 8;  cim.SampleData.r = 8;
cim.setComputationalMode(Numerics.ComputationalMode.MPLoewner, Numerics.RealizationSize(0, 48));
cim.RealizationData.AutoRank = true;

[V, Lam] = cim.eigs();  ew = diag(Lam);
in = c.inside(ew);  ew = ew(in);  V = V(:,in);
res = Numerics.relres(T, ew, V, op.sample_mode);
ok  = res < 1e-8;                                  % trusted eigenpairs
fprintf('Loewner rank %d; %d web modes inside, %d trusted:\n', cim.ResultData.m, numel(ew), nnz(ok));
for k = 1:numel(ew)
    fprintf('   %.8fi   relres %.1e   dist to 8-digit ref %.1e\n', ...
        imag(ew(k)), res(k), min(abs(ew(k) - ew_ref)));
end

The 24 reference eigenvalues are purely imaginary, and the two lowest sit well apart from the rest. Note that the figure plots \( \operatorname{Im} \lambda \) horizontally.

docs.title: Building Data Matrices
docs.text:
In this section, we will explore how to build Hankel and Loewner data matrices using the methods in sploewner and mploewner submodules of Numerics. For both submodules, there are two types of data that can be used:

  1. Exact Data: For ERA/SPLoewner, this is a state-space description of an LTI system, \( S = \left( A, B, C \right) \). For MPLoewner, this is a transfer function \( H \,:\, \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{m \times p} \).
  2. Inexact Data: For all methods, we use a numerical quadrature rule to approximate the exact data, and use this approximation as input.

For the rest of this section, we will utilize the following example LTI systems \( S_i = \left( A_i, B_i, C_i \right), i = 1, 2 \) and their corresponding transfer function:

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = A_i \mathbf{x}(t) + B_i \mathbf{u}(t); \mathbf{y}(t) = C_i \mathbf{x} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad H_i(z) = C_i (zI - A_i)^{-1} B_i \]

where

n = 6; A = diag(-n:-1);
B1 = (1:n)'; C1 = 1:n;
B2 = ones(n,2); C2 = ones(n,2)';
%
H1 = @(z) C1*((z*eye(size(A)) - A) \ B1);
H2 = @(z) C2*((z*eye(size(A)) - A) \ B2);

docs.title: ERA/Single Point Loewner (SPLoewner)
docs.text:
When one expands \( H \) in a Neumann series about \( \sigma = \infty \) (valid for \( \vert z \vert >> 0 \)), the coefficient matrices of this expansion are called Markov parameters of the associated LTI system. If the state-space representation of the system is known, the Markov parameters are given as \( M_k = C A^{k-1} B \) for \( k = 1, 2, \ldots \) For the purposes of minimal system realization/pole identification via the Eigenvalue Realization Algorithm (ERA), it is sufficient to construct the first \( 2K \) Markov parameters, arrange them in an augmented data matrix, and then exact a system \( \hat{S} = \left( \hat{A}, \hat{B}, \hat{C} \right) \) with equivalent dynamics as \( S \).

Choosing \(K\)

The necessary choice of \(K\) will depend on the input/output dimensions of the system, as well as the desired state dimension of the realized system; generically, larger choices of \(K\) will increase the rank of the data matrices, but the impacts of rounding errors or noise due to increasing powers of \(A\) can make larger data matrices diverge from the Hankel operator limit as \( K \rightarrow \infty \). Choosing \(K\) such that \( \text{rank}(\mathbb{D}) \geq \) the McMillan degree of the underlying system will allow for minimal system realization via ERA.

If we consider the SISO system \( S_1 \) from above, we might choose \( K = 5 \), and construct the first \( 2K \) Markov parameters:

K = n; sigma = Inf;
M = Numerics.sploewner.build_exact_moments(sigma,A,B1,C1,2*K);

We can then use these moments to construct the \( 5 \times 5 \) base and shifted data matrices, and try to recover the eigenvalues of \(A\):

[Db,Ds] = Numerics.sploewner.build_sploewner(sigma,M,M,M,K);
norm(eig(Ds,Db)-diag(A)) % 5.8359e-10

If we choose \( \sigma \in \left( \mathbb{C} \setminus \{ \infty \} \right) \), then our expansion of \(H\) about \( \sigma \) will contain coefficient matrices that depend on \( \sigma \) -- these are known as generalized moment matrices of \( S \) at \( \sigma \). The same approach as in the case of ERA can be used to recover the eigenvalues of \(A\):

sigma = 1+1i;
M = Numerics.sploewner.build_exact_moments(sigma,A,B1,C1,2*K);
[Db,Ds] = Numerics.sploewner.build_sploewner(sigma,M,M,M,K);
norm(eig(Ds,Db)-diag(A)) % 1.0300e-04
Choice of \( \sigma \neq \infty \)

The choice of shift \( \sigma \) is crucial for the quality of poles realized in SPLoewner. To see the effect, realize \( S_1 \) on a grid of shifts and compare each realization's pole error against ERA's. The resulting heatmap of the ratio between 2-norm error of ERA and SPLoewner for \( \sigma \in \{ z \in \mathbb{C} \,:\, -10 \leq \mathfrak{R}(z) \leq 5, -7.5 \leq \mathfrak{I}(z) \leq 7.5 \} \) is as follows:

A value greater than 0 indicates that the poles of SPLoewner are increasingly more accurate ERA, while a value less than 0 indicates the opposite. The region of the complex plane in which a finite shift more accurately recovers the poles of \( S_1 \) is highly dependent on the underlying system matrices and size/shape of the formed data matrices.

docs.title: Multi Point Loewner (MPLoewner)
docs.text:
When it is possible to sample the transfer function of a system directly, the MPLoewner method can be used to compute the poles of the system. Data matrices are formed by taking divided differences of the transfer function sampled at left and right sets of interpolation points. For the version of MPLoewner implemented in package, it is assumed that the transfer function is either:

  1. SISO; or,
  2. MIMO with left and right sets of tangential interpolation directions used in constructing entries of the Loewner data matrices.

docs.title: SISO
docs.text:
\( S_1 \) is SISO, so we only need to choose left and right interpolation point sets \( \left( \Theta, \Sigma \right) = \{ (\theta_i,\sigma_i) \,:\, i = 1,2,...,K \} \) such that \( \left( \Theta \cup \Sigma \right) \cap \sigma(A) = \emptyset \) and \( \Theta \cap \Sigma = \emptyset \):

ellt = @(n) (-1)^n*n; rt = @(n) (-1)^(n+1)*n;
theta = 1i*arrayfun(ellt,2:(n+1)); sigma = 1i*arrayfun(rt,2:(n+1));
Choosing left/right interpolation points

For better results with MPLoewner, left/right interpolation points should, ideally, be close to the desired eigenvalues and interleaved; for the latter, this means that \( \vert \theta_i - \sigma_j \vert \) should be relatively small when \( i, j \) are close. This choice of interpolation points biases the ``mass'' of the data matrices towards its diagonal elements and improves corresponding singular value decay.

Then, we can build data matrices \( \mathbb{B} \mathbb{B} \) and \( \mathbb{C} \mathbb{C} \) containing SISO transfer function samples at the left and right interpolation points, and use them to build the base and shifted Loewner data matrices.

[~,BB,~,CC] = Numerics.mploewner.build_exact_data(H1,theta,sigma,1,1);
[Db,Ds] = Numerics.mploewner.build_loewner(BB,CC,theta,sigma);
norm(eig(Ds,Db)-diag(A)) % 5.3235e-07

Note

When calling build_exact_data above, the last two arguments fix the left/right sampling direction to 1 (unscaled).

docs.title: MIMO (with Tangential Interpolation)
docs.text:
When the transfer function corresponds to a MIMO system, one viable strategy is to sample at tangential directions; that is, pick left/right probing directions \( \vec{\ell}/\vec{r} \) corresponding to left and right interpolation points and form Loewner data matrices with scalar samples \( \vec{\ell} H(z) \vec{r} \) instead of matrices \( H(z) \). Random tangential directions are a typical choice for \( \vec{\ell}/\vec{r} \), since the resulting tangentially probed data matrices are unlikely to become rank-deficient in this case.

[~,BB,~,CC] = Numerics.mploewner.build_exact_data(H2,theta,sigma);
[Db,Ds] = Numerics.mploewner.build_loewner(BB,CC,theta,sigma);
norm(eig(Ds,Db)-diag(A)) % 2.1547e-07 -- varries based on tangential directions

docs.title: Inexact Data
docs.text:
In practice, although transfer function samples may be available for some points in \( \mathbb{C} \), the given data may not include transfer function samples at left and right interpolation points, let alone generalized moment data. One approach to dealing with this lack of necessary transfer function samples is to use contour integration and the Cauchy Integral Formula (CIF) to evaluate the underlying transfer function at a specific interpolation point. If \(H\) is a meromorphic matrix-valued function with all of its poles contained within some bounded domain \( \Omega \subset \mathbb{C} \), then we can use contour integration on particular choices of analytic \(f\) to recover useful data about the dynamics of our system. Generally, we perform this contour integration using a numerical quadrature rule on \( \partial \Omega \). For \( \Omega \) conformal to a disk, the trapezoid rule provides exponential convergence guarantees for such data approximations.

First, we create an ellipsoidal contour about the poles of \( H_2 \) with \(8\) quadrature nodes

import Visual.*; % allows us to skip subsequent "Visual."s

c = Contour.Ellipse(-(n+1)/2,n/2,n/4,8);

o = OperatorData(H2); o.refew = diag(A); o.sample_mode = "Direct";

s = SampleData(o,c); s.Contour.plot_quadrature = true;

s.ax = gca;
Contour/Quadrature Visual

We will sketch our evaluations of \(H\) at the quadrature nodes down to \( 1 \times 1 \) moments via a random choice of left/right sketching vectors \( \vec{\ell} / \vec{r} \) and compute the left/right/two-sided moments.

s.ell = 1; s.r = 1; s.compute();

docs.title: ERA/SPLoewner
docs.text:
For ERA, put \( f_k(z) = z^k \) and compute

\[ M_k = C A^k B = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{\partial \Omega} z^k H(z) \, dz \approx \sum_{n=1}^N w_n z_n^k H(z_n). \]

For SPLoewner with \( \sigma \not \in \Omega \), put \( f_k^\sigma(z) = \frac{(-1)^k}{(\sigma - z)^{k+1}} \) and compute

\[ M_k^\sigma = \frac{H^{(k)}(\sigma)}{k!} = \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \oint_{\partial \Omega} \frac{(-1)^k}{(\sigma - z)^{k+1}} H(z) \, dz \approx \sum_{n=1}^N w_n \frac{(-1)^k}{(\sigma - z)^{k+1}} H(z_n). \]

Just as in the case of MPLoewner, we can apply left and right sketching matrices to our quadrature approximation to reduce the size of our approximated quadrature samples.
